entities.name: Dambulla cave temple
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Dambulla Cave Temple (Golden Temple of Dambulla) in central Sri Lanka, carved into a massive rock outcrop rising 160 meters above the surrounding plains, is the largest and best-preserved cave temple complex in Sri Lanka — a UNESCO World Heritage Site (1991) containing 153 Buddha statues, 3 statues of Sri Lankan kings, and 4 statues of gods across five caves, with wall paintings covering 2,100 square meters of ceiling and walls dating from the 1st century BCE through the 18th century CE.

The caves were used as a refuge by King Vattagamani Abhaya (Valagamba) when he fled the Chola invasion in 103 BCE; after recapturing his throne (88 BCE), he transformed the natural caves into a magnificent Buddhist temple complex as an act of thanksgiving. The Royal Cave Temple (Cave II) is the largest — 52 meters long — containing a massive reclining Buddha (15 meters) carved from solid rock, with the ceiling covered in intricate 18th-century paintings depicting the life of the Buddha and scenes from Sri Lankan history.

Dambulla's importance extends beyond its artistic achievement: the site represents 2,100 years of continuous Buddhist worship, making it one of the longest continuously used sacred sites in Asia. The paintings represent five distinct stylistic periods spanning 2,000 years, providing an unbroken visual record of Sri Lankan Buddhist art. The temple is still an active place of worship for Sri Lankan Buddhists, and the pilgrimage up the rock face is one of the island's most important religious acts.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Dambulla Cave Temple — 2,100 years of continuous Buddhist worship, 153 statues and 2,100 square meters of paintings representing Sri Lanka's greatest Buddhist art ensemble, and a UNESCO World Heritage Site — is one of Asia's most important and continuously used sacred cave complexes.
